title: Helios - Private VPC E2E latency surgery & KV-cache/batching lab
summary: Deep technical session focused on private VPC deployment for latency-sensitive payment inference. Covered PrivateLink cross-account setup, NAT/egress considerations, DNS resolver behaviour, MTU and path MTU issues with IPSec tunnels, KV cache warmup and eviction patterns, batching strategies for low-p99 latency, and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with a targeted 50ms p95 on short prompts and to share bench artifacts and network runbooks.
action_items: Alice Park - Share latency benchmark template and previous private-pilot results - 2028-04-15
Ben Ortiz - Provide recommended batching / cache configs to try during pilot (batch size distributions + timeout heuristics) - 2028-04-14
Maya Li - Export current VPC routing table and NAT topology and share with Redwood - 2028-04-13
Priya Nair - Send list of required compliance docs (SOC2 scope, KMS integration requirements) - 2028-04-18
next_steps: Set up pilot project in Redwood Private in Helios VPC (cross-account PrivateLink) week of 2028-04-23
Run synthetic traffic with 50:50 short/long prompt mix to measure p95 and token throughput
Schedule follow-up tuning session (runtime + kernel/quant) after 5 days of pilot
transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-04-11 15:00 UTC | Duration:~73m
Attendees: Alice Park (Redwood AE), Ben Ortiz (Redwood SE), Samira Khan (Redwood), Maya Li (Helios Infra), Tom Raines (Helios CTO), Diego Alvarez (SRE), Priya Nair (Security)

00:00 - Alice (AE): Hey everyone thanks for carving out time. quick agenda: private vpc connectivity, egress models, kv cache behavior, batching/latency tradeoffs, and a short quant discussion. is that right?
00:18 - Maya: yeah that's perfect. main goal is we need <50ms p95 for our short prompt flow (card auth path) and also not leak pii, so private vpc only no public egress.
00:32 - Tom: and timeline is tight, pilot in 2 weeks if we can.
00:40 - Ben (SE): cool, we'll walk through network patterns we've seen — cross-account PrivateLink, endpoint services, or a managed NAT egress — and how they affect runtime requests and TCP reuse.
00:54 - Diego (SRE): quick note: our infra uses AWS across 3 AZs, we currently have one central NAT gateway per AZ, route tables for subnets, and a transit VPC for partner connectivity. we also have an onprem VPN to the colo.
01:12 - Samira: ok, question up front: are you planning to run Redwood Private control plane in Helios VPC or use cross-account endpoints to our Redwood-managed account?
01:25 - Maya: prefer customer-managed control plane in our VPC for auditability, but open to cross-account if we can't finish onprem packaging.
01:36 - Alice: understood. for customer-managed, we recommend cross-account PrivateLink for the runtime calls and a private control plane endpoint in your account. that avoids hairpin NAT and keeps egress minimal.
01:49 - Priya: hairpin? can you explain risks— we have strict egress logging and need mTLS + SNI enforcement.
01:56 - Ben: absolutely. hairpin NAT is when traffic leaves the VPC and comes back, which complicates logs and can break source-IP tracking; PrivateLink keeps traffic within the AWS network plane and supports interface ENIs in your subnets. we also recommend mTLS between your services and the runtime; Redwood supports client certs or SAML for control plane.
02:19 - Tom: what about DNS? our infra uses split-horizon route53 resolver endpoints, we have conditional forwards for internal names. will PrivateLink require special DNS entries?
02:32 - Ben: PrivateLink needs DNS entries pointing to the interface endpoints. typically we create VPC endpoint aliases like runtime-api.redwood.internal -> eni-ip. With split-horizon, you'll want resolver rules or endpoint-specific entries so internal services resolve the endpoint IPs. otherwise you may accidentally resolve to public endpoints.
02:49 - Maya: got it. also concerned about path MTU with our VPN + IPSec to colo. we've seen 1400 MTU reduce throughput and cause fragmentation, any runtime impacts?
03:03 - Ben: yes, path MTU can hurt large payloads: KV cache transfers (checkpoint fetches) during warmup and model weights fetches are big. For steady-state interactive token generation, packets are small, but initial model shard pulls or quant table transfers can get affected. we recommend enabling PMTUD, or adjust MTU on the inside of the IPSec tunnel; also use compressed transfer for weight blobs where possible.
03:26 - Diego: on KV cache — we've got a pattern where our sessions have many short-lived auth checks, so the KV is hit a lot but TTLs are short. what's a good eviction policy?
03:39 - Ben: for that workload we suggest a two-tier KV approach: a short TTL LRU for per-session prefix caching (fast eviction) and a larger persistent cache for warm-start prompts. Redwood's runtime supports prefix-level KV where small keys are pinned for the duration of a session; you can tune the TTL and max-entries per shard. Also watch for cold-starts: you saw p99 spikes when a new model variant loads cache.
04:05 - Alice: can you quantify the p95/p99 impact of a cold KV compared to steady state?
04:12 - Ben: typical numbers: steady state p95 for short prompts ~30-45ms with continuous batching and KV hot; cold KV (first 10 requests) can spike p99 to several seconds while submodels or embeddings are fetched and weights cached. that's why we recommend a warmup traffic pattern or pre-warming with synthetic requests from your infra.
04:30 - Tom: so in practice we pre-warm from our side? won't that add cost?
04:35 - Ben: yes some cost, but you only need small burst traffic to warm KV and weights. for payments flow it's worth it. Redwood can also pre-warm during a canary rollout if you pin versions.
04:44 - Maya: batching — we are nervous about micro-batching delaying single-request latency. our traffic is bursty with occasional batchable background jobs. what's the recommended approach?
04:56 - Ben: micro-batching trades throughput for latency. With continuous batching you get sub-ms amortization on kernels, but you must set maximum batch size and a short batching timeout (e.g., 3-7ms) to keep p95 low. For strict 50ms p95, use a small max batch (4-8) and low timeout, and enable dynamic backpressure so long requests don't block short ones.
05:23 - Diego: any kernel-level tips? quantization choices affect runtime performance, right?
05:28 - Ben: yes. INT8/4-bit quant reduces memory and token cost, but may add dequant/requant overheads depending on kernel fusion on the GPU. Redwood runtime chooses fused kernels when available; for some models we prefer FP16 with optimized attention kernels for p95-sensitive paths. We'll share model-specific quant profiles.
05:45 - Samira: note, model name in our doc is "helios-llm-v1" but transcriber could mess that up.
05:52 - Alice: (laughs) noted.
06:00 - [Timestamp jump - network diagram share]
06:10 - Ben: showing topology: Helios VPC with private subnets for API frontends, PrivateLink interface endpoints in each AZ connecting to Redwood runtime NLBs in Redwood account, control plane private endpoint in-customer-account, cross-account IAM roles for provisioning. Preference: use interface endpoints in the same subnets as your frontends to preserve AZ-local traffic.
06:37 - Maya: how do we handle failover if an ENI is unhealthy?
06:41 - Ben: AWS manages ENI health, but at application level we recommend multi-AZ PrivateLink endpoints and client-side retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Redwood SDK can route to local AZ endpoints to reduce cross-AZ hops.
06:55 - Priya: security: we need audit logs for every inference call and token obfuscation. how are logs surfaced?
07:05 - Alice: Redwood can ship token-level metrics to your SIEM via private Kinesis or S3 (no public egress). payloads are never logged by default; you can opt-in for redaction or PII hashing. Control plane audit logs live in your account if you choose customer-managed control plane.
07:24 - Tom: one of our compliance folks will want to run a penetration test. support that?
07:29 - Samira: yes, Redwood has a standard testing window and a runbook for pentest coordination; Priya we can share the form.
07:38 - Diego: practical debugging: if we see 500s and timeouts, what traces should we pull?
07:43 - Ben: start with the SDK request id, check client-side DNS resolution, client connections (socket reuse), and backend p95. For network-level issues, collect traceroute, MTU results, and ENI flow logs. Redwood's console will show per-route latencies and kernel-level breakdowns (KV lookup, model forward, tokenization).
08:05 - Tom: can we get console access in a read-only demo for our infra folks?
08:09 - Alice: yes we'll spin up a demo with SG-limited read-only role.
08:12 - [Discussion of pilot metrics and SLAs]
08:20 - Ben: pilot plan: 2-week pilot in Helios VPC, run canary on 10% of auth traffic with synthetic warmups, measure p50/p95/p99 per route, and validate KV eviction under session churn. We'll instrument both client and runtime sides.
08:36 - Maya: what's the expected token throughput per instance? we have spikes during batch settlement windows.
08:42 - Ben: depends on model size and quant profile; rough ballpark for mid-sized 30B model with INT8 fused kernels is ~120-200 tokens/sec per GPU core for generation in interactive mode. For small short prompt workloads token rates are less relevant than latency — throughput matters for batch jobs. We'll run sizing test during pilot.
09:05 - Diego: any gotchas with SNI and mTLS when PrivateLink sits in front? we've seen some TLS mismatch errors in past integrations.
09:13 - Samira: ensure your clients set SNI to the PrivateLink alias and that the cert CN/SAN matches. With mTLS also ensure mutual cert validation is enabled on both sides. We recommend terminating TLS in your app and using mTLS to the endpoint if you need end-to-end auth.
09:30 - Maya: in our environment we also have egress proxies for third-party services. will the runtime traffic to the control plane or any add-on call go through that proxy if we choose NAT egress?
09:42 - Ben: yes, if you use NAT egress then outbound control-plane calls will traverse your NAT/proxy. That adds TLS handshake and proxy latency. PrivateLink avoids that. If you must use NAT, route rules and proxy keepalive tuning are critical to avoid handshake overhead for each inference call.
10:03 - Alice: can we go through a failure scenario? say one AZ loses ENI connectivity and our frontends still route, what's the behavior?
10:12 - Ben: runtime is multi-AZ; requests from clients will failover to other AZ endpoints. SDK will retry but you'll see small p95 increases. If the issue is in-path (egress NAT outage) and it blocks access to weights in object store, that can cause larger p99s during model reloads. So ensure object storage access is available via VPC endpoints or replicate model artifacts to local caches.
10:35 - Diego: about caching artifacts — can we pin model shards to local disk on runtime nodes to avoid refetch?
10:41 - Ben: yes, Redwood supports pinned artifacts and local shard persistence; during Dedicated/Private deployments you can mount EBS or local NVMe caches. The service also supports checksum-based cache validation to avoid full downloads on restarts.
10:55 - Maya: earlier you mentioned KV warmup. what's recommended warmup pattern?
11:00 - Ben: run a set of synthetic requests that mimic the prefix distribution of production. For auth flows, hit typical prefixes with expected session lengths. Start with a ramp: low qps but cover all keys, then increase to burst levels. Also use sticky routing so warm caches stay hot per AZ.
11:20 - Tom: will Redwood share scripts for warmup or should we implement our own?
11:25 - Alice: we'll share a warmup harness and the benchmark template. action item.
11:30 - [Brief silence / background typing]
11:42 - Priya: security question: KMS integration for model encryption at rest? we need customer-managed keys.
11:50 - Samira: Redwood Private supports CMK in your account; you can provide the KMS ARN and we integrate key policies into the control plane role. We'll provide a sample IAM policy.
12:05 - Diego: any anomalies you see with packet loss causing inference stalls?
12:10 - Ben: packet loss affects tail latency; recompute increases when you lose retransmitted KV chunks. Monitor retransmits at the OS level and enable TCP keepalive and appropriate RTO. Also watch for competing traffic on the same NIC.
12:27 - Alice: quant question: do you want to run INT8 or FP16 for this pilot?
12:32 - Tom: we prefer to start conservative — stability first — so FP16 maybe. But cost matters.
12:36 - Ben: agreed. start FP16 with tuned attention kernels for latency, then try INT8 in canary to measure p95 delta. We'll provide a small matrix of expected tradeoffs by model.
12:47 - Maya: about observability — can you push detailed per-request spans with KV and kernel timings into our tracing system?
12:57 - Samira: yes, Redwood supports exporting spans to OTLP/Jaeger and we can map fields. We'll share mapping doc.
13:08 - Diego: what about maintenance windows and model rollouts? how do we avoid mass-cache-eviction during a global rollout?
13:16 - Ben: rollout pattern: canary per-AZ then gradual global. Redwood has rollout hooks to pre-warm downstream caches during canary. Also you can set sticky routing to keep some percentage pinned to old variant until warm.
13:33 - Tom: what's the expected effort from Helios infra to get pilot running?
13:37 - Alice: main tasks: create cross-account endpoint role, allocate subnets for interface endpoints, share route tables and NAT topology, and open a small list of ports for internal management. We estimate 2-3 infra days plus a security review.
13:50 - Maya: we'll prioritize.
13:54 - [Wrap up and recap]
14:00 - Alice: recap: Redwood to share bench template, warmup scripts, batching configs, quant profile matrix, and read-only console. Helios to share VPC routing tables and compliance doc list. Pilot kickoff target week of 2028-04-23.
14:15 - Tom: thanks all, this was super helpful.
14:20 - Priya: I'll follow up with the compliance list.
14:25 - Alice: thanks everyone we'll follow up in email with links and the kickoff invite.

End transcript.
